title: Two Tragedies, One Failure: The Absence of Wisdom
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: Anthony Bradley argues that two unrelated news stories share one root failure: nobody was willing to be the wise voice in the room. He defines wisdom as the moral competency to recognize what matters most and choose it under pressure, and says America too often lets profit, convenience, ego and sentimentality make decisions that only wisdom should make. The first case is Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts, who reportedly played and flew across the Atlantic with blood clots in his lungs, which Bradley reads as an industry valuing talent over the body. The second is the Bend, Oregon school shooting, where the weapon was a birthday gift from the shooter's mother to a son reported to have special needs and mental health struggles. Drawing on Warren Farrell and law professor Lynne Marie Kohm, he lists common features of such boys, including little parental involvement, unmanaged stress, long stretches alone, loss of moral truth and lack of remorse. He closes that wisdom is a matter of life and death for anyone entrusted with another person's life.
points: Bradley defines wisdom not as intelligence but as the moral competency to recognize what matters most and choose it under pressure.
He treats the Jalen Hurts blood clot story as an example of an industry and its advisers valuing a player's talent above his body.
In the Oregon shooting he focuses on a parent giving a gun to a struggling teenage son, and asks where the wise adult was.
He argues from Warren Farrell and Lynne Kohm that fatherlessness and parental absence are strong predictors of boys who commit school shootings.
The piece ends on the claim that wisdom is a life-and-death duty for anyone trusted with another human being.
quotes: Wisdom isn’t intelligence. It’s the moral competency to recognize what’s most important and choose it under pressure.

In one situation an entire billion-dollar industry and everyone around a young athlete valued his talent more than his body. In another, a parent gave his son (a child who we’re now told was struggling with mental health issues) a gun.
Some people have liked the NFL to slavery in terms of treating players simply as means an end and this story will most certainly fuel some of the sentiment.
One of the variables that I pay attention to when a teenage boy executes a school shooting is to investigate if he comes from a fatherless home. It seems to be the case in John II’s home.
Here’s what we know: almost every shooting involving a teenage boy develops from a boy who is not emotionally attached to his father.
Wisdom is not the privilege of philosophers and preachers. It is a matter of life and death for anyone who has ever been trusted with the life of another human being.
Until we value wisdom more than wealth, winning, or convenience we will continue to wonder who listened for the wise adult in the room . . . after the harm is done.
